title: WTH is there no distinction between broken and locked entities
text: Simple example: my dishwasher, dryer and washing machines have a button entity for start and one for abort. If it is not running the start button is available and the abort button is unavailable (users in my household including myself read this generally as “broken” or “defective”). If the machine is running the start button is unavailable and the abort button is available. Why is there no state representing “everything is healthy, all is good but this entity is currently not interactable/usable”? Many devices have a lot of entities which are not usable on the regular due to physical device state or simply logical constraints. This would allow automatic dashboards showing all broken entities without including those which are just locked out. 3 posts - 3 participants Read full topic
triage_reason: Recurring workflow gap regarding device states in automation.

title: WTH is there no easy way to check the "lifesigns" of a device?
text: I’m not sure if I have an unusually unstable setup, but a lot of my time with home automation goes into keeping the system alive. Stuff lose connections, needs to be rebooted. You need to realize someone pulled out the wrong USB charger and your sensor died. (Recenly, someone pulled out the IKEA Zigbee repeater, which looks like a USB charger, out of the socket, believing it did nothing. 40% of my Zigbee network were suddenly very unreliable until I could figure out what was wrong.) To combat this, I’ve setup a bunch of “last seen” sensors, on basically every device. Some have built in, but that is typically disabled and need to be enabled. Some custom integration does not. But for each entity belonging to HA, I can get information on when it was last updated. So, for some strange gadgets I have done template sensors which combine all those. But this is all so much workaround for something that should be build-in for HA. Each and every device should have some kind of “lifesign” entry, a synthetic entity that just shows the time when any kind of sign of life was last detected from this device. Ideally, this should be presented in such a way that it easy to extract statistics from it. If a device typically reports in every 10th second, then a 30 second lapse of lifesign might be worthy a notice. If a device typically report every 3rd hour, then a 7 hour lapse might need a notice. I’ve tried setting up a general solution for my setup, but it is basically impossible due to the amount of special coding needed. Yet, all the data is there available inside HA. It should be easy to keep track of the health of your devices, be alerted on network dropouts, lost connections or shaky connections. Let’s make 2027 the year that made administering HA easy! 4 posts - 5 participants Read full topic
triage_reason: Pain point around monitoring device connectivity and health in home setups.

title: Powering an Alpaca trading setup off-grid — how do you size a portable station?
text: I live in Portland, Maine and have been running a small Alpaca trading setup from home — a laptop, a monitor, and my router all need to stay up during outages. I’ve been reading about portable power stations that come with solar generator options and battery power banks, and I’m trying to figure out what would actually be enough for a trading day if the grid goes down. My main uncertainty is sizing. The listings I’ve seen quote capacity in watt-hours and output in watts, but I’m not sure how much headroom to add for a laptop plus monitor plus networking gear kept running for a full session. I’m also wondering whether the pure sine wave output matters for a router or monitor, or whether it only matters for motors and appliances. And there’s the recharge side: if the outage lasts longer than a day, would a modest solar panel realistically top it back up in Maine winter light? If anyone here has actually kept a trading desk running during an outage with one of these, I’d appreciate hearing what capacity worked and what you’d do differently. Still working out the sizing for my laptop, monitor and router, and I’m unsure how much headroom to add for a full trading day. A roundup at Best Portable Power Station of 2026 gave me some capacity comparisons to think about, though I’m not yet sure it settles the Maine winter recharge question. 1 post - 1 participant Read full topic
triage_reason: Trader dealing with power backup and hardware sizing for outages.

title: Feature Request: Expose cart-level custom attributes (and the order note) to post-purchase, `transactioncomplete` and receipt targets
text: Summary POS UI Extensions let an extension write cart-level attributes with shopify.cart.addCartProperties() , and those attributes become the order’s custom attributes. Once the sale completes, however, no POS extension target can read them. The post-purchase targets, the background transactioncomplete event and the receipt block targets all expose line items with their line-level properties, but not the cart-level properties or the order note. We are asking for those to be added. This is unchanged in API version 2026-10. Our Use Case We build POS Cafe, a Shopify POS app for cafés and restaurants. Our extension prints order tickets for the kitchen and bar with the Printing API from the pos.purchase.post.block.render target, and sends orders to kitchen display screens from a pos.app.ready.data transactioncomplete listener. The single most important piece of information on one of those tickets is the table number. Staff choose the table in our tile, and we store it as a cart property ( Table Number ) so it lands on the order as a custom attribute. What the API gives us today (2026-10 type definitions) pos.purchase.post.block.render and pos.purchase.post.action.render receive OrderApi , whose order is { id, name, customerId? } only. The transactioncomplete event ( SaleCompleteEvent ) carries lineItems: LineItem[] with each line’s properties , plus customer, totals, payments, orderId , sourceIdentifier and draftCheckoutUuid . It has no cart properties and no note . pos.receipt-header.block.render and pos.receipt-footer.block.render receive the same transaction data. Cart.properties and Cart.note exist on the Cart API, but the Cart API is only available on cart-scoped targets, so only before the sale completes. Diffing 2026.7 against 2026.10.2, the only additions to the transaction data are sourceIdentifier and taxesIncluded . Why the workarounds are not good enough Fetching the order over the Admin API from our backend after transactioncomplete works, but it adds a network round trip and a server dependency to a ticket that should print within seconds of the sale, and it does nothing when the device is offline, which is exactly when a locally printed ticket matters most. It also means an extension needs backend infrastructure and read_orders scope just to print a table number the device already knew a moment earlier. Copying the attribute onto every line item as a line property is possible, but it duplicates data onto each line, shows up in the Admin order and on customer receipts as line properties, and breaks as soon as a line is added by another app or natively by the merchant rather than through our tile. Reading the cart in a cart-scoped target and caching it in shopify.storage for the post-purchase target is fragile: the targets run in separate sandboxes, the cart can change after our last write, and nothing ties the cached cart to the order that actually completed. What we are asking for Any of the following would solve it, in order of preference: Add properties: Record<string, string> and note?: string to BaseTransactionCompleteEvent / BaseTransactionComplete , so the transactioncomplete event and the receipt targets carry the completed cart’s attributes alongside its line items. Extend OrderApi.order on the post-purchase targets with customAttributes (or properties ) and note , mirroring the Order object in the Admin API. At minimum, make the completed cart’s properties and note available on the post-purchase targets through a read-only snapshot of the cart as it was at checkout. Line-level properties are already exposed on all of these surfaces, so exposing the cart-level equivalent is consistent with the existing contract rather than a new category of data. The attributes are written by extensions in the first place, so no new merchant or customer data is being surfaced. Impact Every POS app that prints or displays anything after the sale, such as kitchen tickets, order numbers for pickup screens, loyalty or fulfilment
triage_reason: Merchant application missing access to cart-level attributes after checkout.
